I have been asked to write for a thousand words about whatever I want, which is a strange kind of permission. Most of the time writing comes with an assignment, a topic, a word count, a deadline, a voice you are supposed to sound like. Here there is none of that, just an open field and a number. A thousand words is long enough to get lost in, but short enough that you feel you should be careful. It is the length of a decent conversation, a short story that forgot its plot, a letter you never send. I find myself thinking about the kitchen at 3 a.m., because that is where unassigned thoughts tend to live.

The kitchen light is the kind that hums. The refrigerator exhales cold air every few minutes and the clock on the microwave blinks 12:00 because the power went out last week and nobody bothered to reset it. I am standing there in socks that don't match, holding a mug with tea gone cold. There is a bowl of leftover rice on the counter, a banana that has gone brown at the stem, a note from myself to myself that says 'buy milk' in a handwriting I don't recognize. The apartment is quiet except for the traffic four stories down, a soft, constant shushing. I think about how often we live in the in-between hours when the world is not demanding anything from us, and how quickly we fill the space with worry or scrolling.

Next door, Mrs. Alvarez always keeps her TV on low volume. I can hear the murmurs through the wall, a Spanish news program, a laugh track, sometimes a telenovela sigh. I have never met her. I know she has a cat because once I saw it on the fire escape, a gray tabby staring at the pigeons like they owed it money. I wonder what she thinks about at 3 a.m. Maybe she is also in her kitchen, maybe she is praying, maybe she is awake because the medication keeps her that way. The building is full of these parallel insomnias, each person carrying their own small private world that presses lightly against the drywall. We assume solitude is isolation, but really it is just crowded in a different way.

The city outside is not sleeping either. Delivery scooters zip under the streetlight, their red taillights smearing across wet asphalt. Somewhere a dog barks and is answered by another dog two blocks over. The air smells faintly of exhaust and the bakery on the corner that starts early. I like that the city never pretends to be asleep. It just changes tempo. The daytime city is loud and transactional; the night city is a different kind of busy, more honest about its needs. People are taking out trash, watering plants, arguing quietly on balconies. It is the city's maintenance hours.

Language feels different at night. The words I know in the daytime have edges; at night they go soft. I think about the word 'hush' and how it contains the sound it describes. I think about 'lullaby' and how it is a lie and a promise at the same time. I think about all the words we use to describe light when really we are always describing the absence of darkness. Maybe that is why insomnia is so fertile. The brain is trying to name things that have no name, to file them away properly. It is an archivist with a broken filing cabinet.

I have a memory of being seven and staying up late with my grandmother while the adults slept. She let me help her make tea with too much sugar, and she told me stories about the country she left. She never said it was sad. She said it was heavy. Heavy like a suitcase you carry for years and then one day you set it down and realize your shoulders have forgotten how to be level. I think about that when I look at my own apartment, at the boxes in the corner that have been there since I moved in three years ago. I am still carrying things I don't need.

The internet is also awake. If I open my phone, the feed will be full of people who are also awake, posting photos of their cats, their coffee, their thoughts in lowercase. It is a kind of collective insomnia, a global 3 a.m. where everyone is trying to be seen without being interrupted. I sometimes feel guilty for not sleeping, as if sleep is a moral achievement. But maybe wakefulness is its own form of care. Maybe staying up is how we keep watch over the things we love, even if we don't know how to protect them yet.

There is a tree outside my window that I have watched for two seasons now. In summer it was full and noisy with leaves. In winter it was a skeleton. Now in early spring it is doing that hesitant thing where buds appear and disappear depending on the night temperature. It is learning again how to be green. I like watching it because it does not hurry. It does not post updates. It just waits for the conditions to be right, and then it tries again. That feels like a kind of wisdom we have forgotten in favor of productivity.

Writing for a thousand words without a prompt is a way of listening to yourself. You start with one thought and it pulls a thread. The thread leads to a kitchen, to a neighbor, to a tree, to a grandmother. It is all connected if you let it be. The point is not to arrive anywhere impressive. The point is to notice the way your mind moves when no one is grading it. I think that is why people keep journals, and why some people talk to themselves in the shower. We need a place where the sentence can be unfinished and that is okay.

I am going to put the mug in the sink now. The tea is cold, but that is fine. The clock still says 12:00. Mrs. Alvarez's TV has gone quiet. The tree is still there, patient. I have written about nine hundred and ninety eight words, give or take, about a night that hasn't ended yet. Maybe that is enough. Maybe the rest is just silence, which is also a kind of writing. If you are reading this at 3 a.m., I hope your socks match. If they don't, I hope you like them that way.

"Language feels different at night. The words I know in the daytime have edges; at night they go soft. I think about the word 'hush' and how it contains the sound it describes.
